Passage: L'Orfeo (SV 318) (Italian pronunciation: [lorˈfɛːo]), sometimes called La favola d'Orfeo [la ˈfaːvola dorˈfɛːo], is a late Renaissance/early Baroque favola in musica, or opera, by Claudio Monteverdi, with a libretto by Alessandro Striggio. It is based on the Greek legend of Orpheus, and tells the story of his descent to Hades and his fruitless attempt to bring his dead bride Eurydice back to the living world. It was written in 1607 for a court performance during the annual Carnival at Mantua. While Jacopo Peri's Dafne is generally recognised as the first work in the opera genre, and the earliest surviving opera is Peri's Euridice, L'Orfeo is the earliest that is still regularly performed.
By the early 17th century the traditional intermedio—a musical sequence between the acts of a straight play—was evolving into the form of a complete musical drama or "opera". Monteverdi's L'Orfeo moved this process out of its experimental era and provided the first fully developed example of the new genre. After its initial performance the work was staged again in Mantua, and possibly in other Italian centres in the next few years. Its score was published by Monteverdi in 1609 and again in 1615. After the composer's death in 1643 the opera went unperformed for many years, and was largely forgotten until a revival of interest in the late 19th century led to a spate of modern editions and performances. At first these performances tended to be concert (unstaged) versions within institutes and music societies, but following the first modern dramatised performance in Paris, in 1911, the work began to be seen in theatres. After the Second World War many recordings were issued, and the opera was increasingly staged in opera houses, although some leading venues resisted it. In 2007, the quatercentenary of the premiere was celebrated by performances throughout the world.
In his published score Monteverdi lists around 41 instruments to be deployed, with distinct groups of instruments used to depict particular scenes and characters. Thus strings, harpsichords and recorders represent the pastoral fields of Thrace with their nymphs and shepherds, while heavy brass illustrates the underworld and its denizens. Composed at the point of transition from the Renaissance era to the Baroque, L'Orfeo employs all the resources then known within the art of music, with particularly daring use of polyphony. The work is not orchestrated as such; in the Renaissance tradition instrumentalists followed the composer's general instructions but were given considerable freedom to improvise.

Text: so i'm a longtime retail worker, but i've always been a bit reserved at the job. i'm not one of those mindless drones that communicate through grunts while tapping on a cellphone, i've always given excellent customer service, but having idle unrelated conversation with strangers is not my forte.

anyway, today an older lady comes up to my register. the interactions, as i've had a thousand times before, proceeded as thus:

me: "hi, how are you?"

customer: "i'm quite well, and yourself?"

"i'm doing alright. did you find everything okay?"

"yes, i did."

"great. your total comes to $8,000,000.12."

"alright."  *pulls out a $8,000,000 bill* "now i know i have the 12 cents in here somewhere..."

this part, as i've seen before, involves the customer upending her change purse on my counter to search for the dime and two pennies. only a problem if there's a line, and on this day there was not. she slowly put surely locates a penny, and shifts it towards me. she spots a dime, and does the same. her eyesight, faded but still useful, hones in on the final copper piece, yet her fingers betray her. she accidentally presses down on a small blister packet of medicine, which she begins to push towards her destination before realizing her mistake.

"oops, that's my medicine. you don't want that, i don't think."

on a normal day, i would say "no, not really" in a gentle tone that conveyed a serious response without being disrespectful. perhaps i would just say "nah" or a small grunt, as we both knew the answer and a response would frankly be useless. but not today. today i decided to play the "yes, and" game, to take the worthless conversation further. today i was going to try to be a real person.

"hah, well it depends, is it anything good?" i replied, hoping to make the joking stance that i would gladly accept oxycontin or vicodin in lieu of a penny. i've never used a recreational drug in my life, but today, just today, i would play the part for the sake of brightening up an old lady's day. i expected a smiling "no" in response, or perhaps an "it's mine!"

but instead of this so-far pleasant foray into prattling continuing, this customer decided to inform me was the medication truly was. she told me it was immodium, the popular anti-diarrheal medication. she proceeded to talk at length, with sentences i shall not repeat, about exactly what causes her to need immodium, and why she carries a dose around everywhere. minute after minute went by, as i silently prayed to the god i lost faith in for something, anything, to distract us. a customer, a robber, a deadly asteroid, please let this onslaught of aural torture end. and end it did, a solid 5 minutes later, with the last remaining wisps of my innocence gone, and my affability dead before it was born.

never again.
